title: Git, GitHub, SDLC, and Software Design Patterns
description: Learn the process and design fundamentals every software team relies on: Git version control, GitHub collaboration workflows, the software development lifecycle, and classic creational and structural design patterns.
objectives: Track changes safely with Git's core commands
Collaborate through branches, pull requests, and conflict resolution
Explain each phase of the software development lifecycle
Apply Agile practices to plan and run work
Recognize and apply common creational and structural design patterns

modules.title: Git Version Control
modules.description: Track changes with commits, isolate work with branches, and undo mistakes safely.
modules.completionCriteria: Initialize a repository, commit work across two branches, and recover from a mistaken change using restore, reset, or revert.

lessons.title: Snapshots with Git
objectives: Initialize a repository and make commits
Read status, diff, and log output

content.introduction: Git records snapshots of your project. Each commit is a permanent checkpoint you can name, inspect, and return to.
content.explanation: Three areas drive everything: the working directory (your files), the staging area (what the next commit will contain), and the repository history (committed snapshots). git add moves changes into staging, git commit turns staging into a permanent snapshot, and git status tells you where a file sits. Commits should be small and single-purpose with imperative messages — 'Add job search filters', not 'stuff' — because history is how teammates understand what changed and why.

examples.title: First commits in a new repository
examples.code:
mkdir job-board && cd job-board
git init
echo "# Job Board" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit"
echo "## Usage" >> README.md
git status
git diff
git add README.md
git commit -m "Document usage"
git log --oneline
examples.walkthrough: init creates the repository, add stages a snapshot, commit records it. status and diff show what is unstaged before you commit, and log --oneline lists the checkpoints you have made.

content.useCase: Every code change you ever want to share, review, or roll back.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does git add do?
options: Stages changes for the next commit
knowledgeCheck.explanation: add copies changes into the staging area; commit then records that snapshot.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which command shows committed history?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: log lists commits newest-first; status shows the working tree and diff shows unstaged changes.

content.summary: Working directory, staging area, repository. Add to stage, commit to record, status and log to inspect.

lessons.title: Branching for Features
objectives: Create and switch between branches
Merge a finished branch back

content.introduction: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Branching lets you build a feature without touching the stable code on main.
content.explanation: git switch -c creates a branch and moves you onto it, so new commits advance that pointer while main stays put. When the work is done, you switch back to main and merge the feature branch in. Merging with --no-ff keeps an explicit merge commit, which makes the branch structure visible in history and lets you revert the whole feature as one unit. Deleting the branch afterward keeps the list of pointers honest.

examples.title: Feature branch to merge
examples.code:
git switch -c feature/job-search
# ...edit files...
git add -p
git commit -m "Add job search filters"
git switch main
git pull
git merge --no-ff feature/job-search
git branch -d feature/job-search
git push origin main
git log --oneline --graph -8
examples.walkthrough: Work happens on the feature branch, main is updated with a pull first, --no-ff records the merge, and the merged branch is deleted once its commits live on main.

content.useCase: Building any feature or fix without destabilizing the code everyone else is using.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does git switch -c do?
options: Creates a branch and checks it out
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The -c flag creates the new branch and switches to it in one step.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why branch at all instead of committing to main?
options: It isolates unfinished work so main stays stable and reviewable
knowledgeCheck.explanation: main stays deployable while work proceeds and gets reviewed on the branch.

content.summary: Branch to isolate work, commit there, merge back into main, and delete the branch when done.

lessons.title: Undoing Work Safely
objectives: Choose between restore, reset, and revert
Stash unfinished work

content.introduction: Mistakes are normal in Git. The important skill is picking the right undo — the answer depends on whether the change is staged, committed, or already pushed.
content.explanation: To throw away local edits, use git restore. To unstage, restore --staged. To undo the latest local commit but keep its changes, reset --soft HEAD~1. To undo a commit that has already been pushed, never rewrite history — use git revert, which adds a new commit that inverse-applies the old one, keeping everyone else's clones valid. When you need to pause work mid-task, stash saves your changes aside and lets you pop them back later.

examples.title: Choosing an undo command
examples.code:
git restore --staged src/app.js     # unstage, keep edits
git restore src/app.js             # discard local edits
git reset --soft HEAD~1            # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git stash push -m "wip filters"    # park unfinished work
git stash pop                      # bring it back
git revert a1b2c3d                 # undo a pushed commit with a new commit
examples.walkthrough: Each line targets a different point: working tree, staging area, local history, or shared history. The rule of thumb — rewrite what is local, revert what is shared.

content.useCase: Fixing a wrong file, uncommitting a premature message, or cleaning up a commit before a review.

knowledgeCheck.question: How do you undo a commit that has already been pushed?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Revert adds a new commit that reverses the change, so shared history is never rewritten.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does git stash let you do?
options: Park unfinished changes so you can switch tasks and restore them later
knowledgeCheck.explanation: stash clears the working tree temporarily; pop or apply brings the changes back.

content.summary: Restore discards, reset rewrites local commits, revert undoes pushed ones, and stash pauses work.

modules.title: Collaboration & GitHub Workflows
modules.description: Work with a team through remote branches, pull requests, and conflict resolution.
modules.completionCriteria: Push a feature branch, open and merge a pull request, and resolve a merge conflict without losing either side's work.

lessons.title: The Feature Branch Workflow
objectives: Clone a remote repository
Push a feature branch with an upstream

content.introduction: A remote such as GitHub is the shared copy of the repository. Everyone clones it, branches from it, and pushes their work back.
content.explanation: clone copies the full history once. From then on you work on a branch and push it with -u, which sets the upstream so later git push and git pull know their default target. The core loop is: pull main to get teammates' work, create a branch, commit, push, open a pull request. Never push directly to main on a shared repository — it bypasses review and breaks anyone mid-clone.

examples.title: Clone, branch, push
examples.code:
git clone https://github.com/acme/job-board.git
cd job-board
git switch -c feature/job-search
git pull origin main          # start from the latest shared code
# ...edit, add, commit...
git push -u origin feature/job-search
git status                    # shows branch and upstream
examples.walkthrough: The -u flag links your local branch to the remote one, so after the first push, plain git push sends your commits to the right place.

content.useCase: Any team repository where more than one person commits code.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does git clone produce?
options: A full local copy with history and a remote configured
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Clone includes all commits and sets origin as the default remote.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why push with -u the first time?
options: It sets the upstream so later push and pull know the default target
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Without an upstream, every push needs explicit remote and branch arguments.

content.summary: Clone once, branch per feature, pull before you start, and push with -u to link the upstream.

lessons.title: Pull Requests and Code Review
objectives: Open a pull request that explains the change
Merge after review and checks

content.introduction: A pull request is a proposal: 'these commits should be merged, here is why.' It is where review and automated checks happen.
content.explanation: A good pull request is small, links the issue it closes, and describes both what changed and how to test it. Reviewers comment on the diff before it lands; on GitHub you can approve, request changes, or leave suggestions. Required status checks — linting and tests — must pass before merging, which is what stops a broken build from reaching main. Squash merging keeps history linear by collapsing the branch into one commit with a clean message.

examples.title: Opening and merging a PR from the CLI
examples.code:
git push -u origin feature/job-search
gh pr create --title "Add job search filters" --body "Closes #12"
gh pr checks                      # wait for CI to pass
gh pr diff                       # review the exact changes
gh pr review --approve            # record approval
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch
examples.walkthrough: The PR description closes the tracking issue automatically, checks gate the merge, and --squash --delete-branch leaves one clean commit on main and removes the feature branch.

content.useCase: Merging any feature, fix, or refactor into a shared branch.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main purpose of a pull request?
options: To propose and review changes before merging
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It is a reviewable proposal with discussion, checks, and an approval trail.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why require CI checks to pass before merging?
options: To prevent broken or failing code from reaching main
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Automated tests and linting catch regressions before they land.

content.summary: Small PRs with linked issues, review comments, green checks, and a squash merge keep history clean.

lessons.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
objectives: Recognize and resolve conflict markers
Choose between merge and rebase

content.introduction: A conflict means Git cannot decide which change to keep — both branches edited the same lines. Git stops and makes you choose.
content.explanation: When a merge stops, the file contains marker blocks: <<<<<<< yours, =======, and >>>>>>> theirs, with your version first. You edit the file into the state you actually want, delete the markers, stage it, and commit. Two workflows avoid surprises: merge preserves the true history including branches and is safe for shared repositories, while rebase replays your commits on top of the latest main for a linear history — but rebasing rewrites commits, so never rebase anything already pushed. When a merge goes sideways, git merge --abort returns you to where you started.

examples.title: Walking through a conflict
examples.code:
git switch main && git pull
git merge feature/job-search
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/app.js
git status
# edit src/app.js: keep what you want, remove <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> lines
git add src/app.js
git commit -m "Resolve conflict in app.js"

# start over instead:
git merge --abort
examples.walkthrough: status points at the conflicted files, you resolve by hand, staging the file tells Git the conflict is settled, and commit finishes the merge. abort is the escape hatch.

content.useCase: Two people editing the same function, or a long-lived branch returning to an active main.

knowledgeCheck.question: What do the <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers mean?
options: Both branches changed the same region and you must choose the final content
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The markers bracket each side's version; you edit the region into the correct result.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is it safe to rebase?
options: On local commits that have not been pushed
On any commit in a shared repository
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Rebase rewrites commit ids; doing it to pushed work diverges from everyone else's history.

content.summary: Conflicts are your decision to make: edit, stage, commit — or abort and try again.

modules.title: Software Development Lifecycle
modules.description: How software is planned, built, tested, released, and maintained as a repeatable process.
modules.completionCriteria: Describe each SDLC phase for a real feature and map it onto an Agile sprint with an automated test and deployment step.

lessons.title: Phases of the SDLC
objectives: Name and order the SDLC phases
Explain the output of each phase

content.introduction: The software development lifecycle is the sequence of phases a team moves through to plan, build, release, and maintain a product.
content.explanation: Requirements gather what and why — user stories with acceptance criteria. Design decides how: architecture, data models, interfaces. Implementation turns designs into code. Verification tests against the requirements, not just the code. Deployment ships it to users. Maintenance is the longest phase: monitoring, bug fixes, and iterations based on real feedback. The phases are not strictly one-way — feedback loops send teams back to design or requirements, which is why the cycle is drawn as a loop rather than a line.

examples.title: One iteration through the lifecycle
examples.walkthrough: Each line is a phase with a concrete artifact — requirements, design doc, code, test results, review, release, telemetry — and the final line feeds real-world feedback into the next round of planning.

content.useCase: Any feature from idea to production, from a two-person app to an enterprise release.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which phase defines what the software must do and why?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Requirements capture user needs and acceptance criteria before design begins.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is the SDLC drawn as a cycle rather than a line?
options: Because phases are skipped in practice
Because feedback from use sends the team back to requirements and design
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Real products iterate; maintenance and user feedback drive the next improvements.

content.summary: Requirements, design, implementation, verification, deployment, maintenance — with feedback loops between them.

lessons.title: Agile and Scrum Cadence
objectives: Explain backlog, sprint, and ceremony roles
Run a short inspection loop

content.introduction: Agile replaces big up-front plans with short iterations that deliver working software and respond to change.
content.explanation: Work lives in a product backlog — a prioritized list of user stories. A sprint is a fixed time box, typically one or two weeks, in which the team commits to a sprint goal and pulls in what it can finish. Daily standups sync progress and surface blockers, the sprint review demos done work, and the retrospective asks what to improve. The team is self-organizing: estimates come from the people doing the work, and the product owner owns priority.

examples.title: A sprint as a small state machine
examples.walkthrough: Cards flow across the board, the daily standup keeps blockers visible, and the sprint closes with a demo and a retrospective before the next goal is set.

content.useCase: Any team delivering software incrementally instead of one large release at the end.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a sprint?
options: A fixed time box for delivering an increment of work
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Sprints are short, bounded iterations that end with demonstrated, working software.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of the retrospective?
options: To inspect how the team worked and decide what to improve
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The demo is about the product; the retrospective is about the process and the team.

content.summary: Prioritized backlog, time-boxed sprints, daily syncs, demo, retrospective — working software every iteration.

lessons.title: Testing and CI in the Lifecycle
objectives: Place unit, integration, and e2e tests in the pipeline
Read a basic CI workflow

content.introduction: Verification is only useful if it runs on every change. Continuous integration turns testing into an automatic gate rather than a manual chore.
content.explanation: Tests are layered by cost and scope: unit tests are fast and check one function, integration tests exercise routes and databases, and end-to-end tests drive a real browser through a user journey. CI runs the cheap layers first so failures surface in seconds, then the expensive ones. A pipeline that runs on every push and pull request means broken code is caught in minutes, before it can reach main — which is exactly the verification phase of the SDLC made continuous.

examples.title: A GitHub Actions CI workflow
examples.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run test:e2e
examples.walkthrough: Every push and PR triggers a clean checkout, a pinned Node version, and a dependency install, followed by linting, unit tests, and end-to-end tests in order of increasing cost.

content.useCase: Protecting main from regressions on any project with automated tests.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why run unit tests before end-to-end tests in CI?
options: Unit tests are faster, so failures show up sooner
E2E tests cannot run in CI
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cheap checks first give the fastest feedback; slow browser tests run only after they pass.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does continuous integration actually integrate?
options: Each developer's changes into the shared mainline, verified by automated tests
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Frequent merges with automated verification keep the shared branch in a working state.

content.summary: Layer tests from fast to slow, run them automatically on every change, and treat green CI as the gate to main.

modules.title: Creational & Structural Design Patterns
modules.description: Proven solutions for creating objects and composing them into larger structures.
modules.completionCriteria: Identify a repeated design problem in existing code and apply Singleton, Factory, Builder, or Adapter to solve it without changing how callers use it.

lessons.title: Singleton and Factory
objectives: Limit a class to one shared instance
Create objects through a factory function

content.introduction: Design patterns are named solutions to problems that recur across projects. Two creational patterns you will meet early control how objects come into existence.
content.explanation: Singleton guarantees a single shared instance — appropriate for genuinely one-per-process resources like a database connection or logger, and a poor fit for state you might want isolated per test. A factory hides construction behind a function: callers describe what they want and the factory decides which concrete object to return. Factories keep creation logic in one place, so adding a new variant means editing the factory instead of hunting construction sites through the codebase.

examples.title: Singleton connection and a notifier factory
examples.walkthrough: getDb returns the same connection every call instead of opening new ones. notify maps a channel name to the right sender, so callers never construct notifiers themselves.

content.useCase: Shared infrastructure objects (connections, loggers) and pluggable variants (payment or notification channels).

knowledgeCheck.question: What problem does the Singleton pattern solve?
options: Ensuring only one instance exists for a shared resource
knowledgeCheck.explanation: One process-wide instance prevents duplicate connections or conflicting state.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main benefit of a factory function?
options: It removes the need for classes everywhere
It centralizes creation logic so variants change in one place
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Callers ask for an outcome; the factory owns the decision about what to build.

content.summary: Singleton owns one shared instance; a factory owns creation logic so variants stay in one place.

lessons.title: Prototype and Builder
objectives: Reuse objects through prototypes
Construct complex objects step by step

content.introduction: When construction takes several steps or you want cheap copies of existing objects, Prototype and Builder keep the calling code clean.
content.explanation: Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing one — in JavaScript this is the language's core mechanism: Object.create delegates to a prototype, and {...obj} makes a shallow copy, which is far cheaper than re-running a constructor for every item. Builder assembles a complex object step by step through chained calls, then hands over a finished value. It shines when construction has many optional parts, because a builder makes the order and defaults explicit instead of a long positional argument list.

examples.title: A chainable query builder
examples.walkthrough: Each method returns this, so calls chain readably, and build() produces the final value with sensible defaults — no constructor with ten optional parameters.

content.useCase: Query builders, report configuration, and copying template objects with per-item tweaks.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is the Builder pattern most useful?
options: When an object needs many optional construction steps
When an object has no fields
When you need to delete an object
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Chained steps replace long, error-prone argument lists for complex objects.

knowledgeCheck.question: How does JavaScript's prototype mechanism create objects?
options: By compiling classes ahead of time
By delegating property lookups to a shared prototype object
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Objects inherit behavior from their prototype, which is why {...obj} can cheaply copy and extend one.

content.summary: Prototype reuses existing objects by copying; Builder constructs complex values step by step with explicit defaults.

lessons.title: Adapter and Decorator
objectives: Wrap incompatible interfaces with an adapter
Add behavior by stacking decorators

content.introduction: Structural patterns are about composing objects. Adapter makes an awkward interface fit yours; Decorator adds behavior without modifying the original.
content.explanation: An Adapter translates one interface into another the rest of your code expects, so a legacy SDK, a third-party API, or a differently shaped service can be swapped in behind a stable call. That translation lives in exactly one class. Decorators wrap an object and extend it — each one adds a single concern such as logging, caching, or auth. Stacking small decorators beats a monolithic wrapper, and it is the same idea behind Express middleware: each function wraps the next and adds one behavior.

examples.title: Adapting a legacy XML service
examples.walkthrough: The rest of the application calls billing.getInvoice(id) and receives a plain object; only the adapter knows about XML, so replacing the legacy service means changing one class.

content.useCase: Integrating third-party SDKs, wrapping legacy code, and adding logging or auth around a call.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does an Adapter do?
options: Converts one interface into another the caller expects
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It translates calls and data so an incompatible dependency fits your codebase.

knowledgeCheck.question: How does a Decorator add behavior?
options: By editing the original class source
By wrapping the object and extending it around the original calls
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Wrapping keeps the original untouched, so decorators stack independently — like Express middleware.

content.summary: Adapter translates foreign interfaces to yours; Decorator wraps objects to add one concern at a time.
